title.fr: Cendrillon ou la Petite Pantoufle de verre
title.en: Cinderella, or the Little Glass Slipper
title.pt: A Gata Borralheira ou o Sapatinho de Cristal

en: Once upon a time there was a gentleman who took as his second wife the haughtiest and proudest woman anyone had ever seen.
She had two daughters of the same temper, who were like her in every way.
The husband, for his part, had a young daughter, but of unequalled kindness; she got that from her mother, who had been the best person in the world.
The wedding was no sooner over than the stepmother let her bad temper show: she couldn't bear the good qualities of this young girl, which made her own daughters look even more hateful.
She gave her the lowest jobs in the house: it was she who cleaned the dishes and the stairs, who scrubbed madam's room and the rooms of the young ladies, her daughters;

she slept right at the top of the house, in an attic, on a wretched straw mattress, while her sisters had rooms with parquet floors, where they had the most fashionable beds and mirrors in which they could see themselves from head to toe.
The poor girl put up with everything patiently and didn't dare complain to her father, who would have scolded her, because his wife ruled him completely.
When she had finished her work, she would go and sit in the corner by the fireplace, among the cinders, which is why she was usually called Cinderbottom.
The younger sister, who wasn't as rude as the elder, called her Cinderella.
Yet Cinderella, in her shabby clothes, was still a hundred times more beautiful than her sisters, even though they were dressed very magnificently.
It happened that the king's son gave a ball and invited all the people of rank.
Our two young ladies were invited too, for they cut quite a figure in the land.
There they were, delighted and very busy choosing the dresses and hairstyles that would suit them best.
More work for Cinderella; for she was the one who ironed her sisters' linen and pleated their cuffs.
People talked of nothing but how they would dress.
"I," said the elder, "will wear my red velvet dress with my English lace trimming."
"I," said the younger, "will only have my ordinary skirt; but to make up for it, I'll wear my cloak with gold flowers and my diamond necklace, which is far from ordinary."
They sent for the best hairdresser to set up their double-row headdresses, and bought beauty spots from the best maker.
They called Cinderella to ask her opinion, because she had good taste.
Cinderella gave them the best advice in the world and even offered to do their hair, which they were glad to accept.
While she was doing their hair, they said to her: Cinderella, would you like to go to the ball?
"Alas, young ladies, you're making fun of me; that's not the place for me."
"You're right; people would laugh if they saw a Cinderbottom going to the ball."
Anyone other than Cinderella would have done their hair badly on purpose; but she was kind, and she did it perfectly.
They went almost two days without eating, they were so carried away with joy.
More than a dozen laces were broken from pulling them tight to make their waists slimmer, and they were always in front of their mirror.
At last the happy day arrived: they set off, and Cinderella followed them with her eyes for as long as she could.
When she could no longer see them, she began to cry.
Her godmother, who saw her in tears, asked her what was the matter.
"I would so like to…"
She was crying so hard that she couldn't finish.
Her godmother, who was a fairy, said to her: You would like to go to the ball, wouldn't you?
"Alas, yes," said Cinderella with a sigh.
"Well then, will you be a good girl?" said her godmother. "I'll get you there."
She took her into her room and said to her: Go into the garden and bring me a pumpkin.
Cinderella went at once to pick the finest one she could find and brought it to her godmother, unable to guess how this pumpkin could get her to the ball.
Her godmother hollowed it out and, leaving only the skin, struck it with her wand, and the pumpkin was immediately changed into a beautiful golden carriage;
then she went to look in the mousetrap, where she found six mice, all alive.

She told Cinderella to lift the door of the mousetrap a little, and as each mouse came out, she gave it a tap with her wand, and the mouse was immediately changed into a fine horse, which made a splendid team of six horses of a lovely dappled mouse grey.
As she was wondering what to make a coachman from, Cinderella said: I'll go and see if there's a rat in the rat trap; we can make a coachman of it.
"You're right," said her godmother, "go and look."
Cinderella brought her the rat trap, which had three big rats in it.
The fairy chose one of the three, because of his splendid whiskers; and when she had touched him, he was changed into a fat coachman with one of the finest moustaches ever seen.
Then she said to her: Go into the garden; you'll find six lizards behind the watering can; bring them to me.

No sooner had she brought them than her godmother changed them into six footmen, who immediately climbed up behind the carriage in their braided uniforms and held on as if they had never done anything else in their lives.
The fairy then said to Cinderella: Well! There's what you need to go to the ball; aren't you pleased?
"Yes, but am I to go like this, in my ugly clothes?"
Her godmother just touched her with her wand, and at once her clothes were changed into a dress of gold and silver cloth, all covered with jewels;
then she gave her a pair of glass slippers, the prettiest in the world.

When she was dressed like this, she got into the carriage, but her godmother warned her above all not to stay past midnight, telling her that if she stayed at the ball one moment longer, her carriage would become a pumpkin again, her horses mice, her footmen lizards, and her old clothes would go back to the way they were.
She promised her godmother that she would be sure to leave the ball before midnight.
Off she goes, beside herself with joy.
The king's son, who was told that a great princess nobody knew had just arrived, ran to welcome her;
he gave her his hand as she stepped down from the carriage and led her into the hall where everyone was.
Then a great silence fell; the dancing stopped and the violins played no more, so intent was everyone on gazing at the great beauty of this stranger.
All you could hear was a confused murmur: Ah, how beautiful she is!
Even the king, old as he was, couldn't stop looking at her and whispering to the queen that it had been a long time since he had seen such a beautiful and charming person.
All the ladies were busy studying her hair and her clothes, so as to have the same ones the very next day, provided they could find fabrics fine enough and workers skilled enough.
The king's son gave her the seat of honour, and then took her to dance.
She danced so gracefully that everyone admired her even more.
A very fine supper was served, of which the young prince ate nothing, he was so busy gazing at her.
She went and sat beside her sisters and was very gracious to them:
she shared with them the oranges and lemons the prince had given her, which surprised them greatly, for they didn't recognise her at all.
While they were admiring her like this, Cinderella heard the clock strike a quarter to twelve: she immediately made a deep curtsy to the company and left as fast as she could.
As soon as she got home, she went to find her godmother; and after thanking her, she told her she would very much like to go to the ball again the next day, because the king's son had asked her to.
As she was busy telling her godmother everything that had happened at the ball, the two sisters knocked at the door: Cinderella went to open it.
"How long you've been!" she said to them, yawning, rubbing her eyes and stretching as if she had only just woken up.
Yet she hadn't felt like sleeping at all since they had parted.
"If you had come to the ball," one of her sisters said to her, "you wouldn't have been bored:
the most beautiful princess came, the most beautiful anyone could ever see;
she was very gracious to us, she gave us oranges and lemons."
Cinderella was beside herself with joy.
She asked them the princess's name; but they told her that nobody knew her;
that the king's son was very troubled about it, and that he would give anything in the world to know who she was.
Cinderella smiled and said to them: So she was very beautiful!
Goodness, how lucky you are!
Couldn't I see her?
Oh, Miss Javotte, please lend me your yellow dress, the one you wear every day.
"Really!" said Miss Javotte. "What an idea!
Lend my dress to a filthy Cinderbottom like you! I'd have to be quite mad."
Cinderella fully expected this refusal, and was glad of it; for she would have been in a real fix if her sister had agreed to lend her the dress.
The next day the two sisters went to the ball, and Cinderella too, but dressed even more splendidly than the first time.
The king's son stayed by her side the whole time and never stopped whispering sweet words to her.
The young lady was far from bored, and forgot what her godmother had told her;
so much so that she heard the first stroke of midnight when she thought it wasn't even eleven yet;
she got up and fled as nimbly as a deer.
The prince followed her, but he couldn't catch her.
She dropped one of her glass slippers, which the prince picked up very carefully.

Cinderella arrived home quite out of breath, without carriage, without footmen, and in her shabby clothes, with nothing left of all her finery but one of her little slippers, the twin of the one she had dropped.
The guards at the palace gate were asked if they had seen a princess leave:
they said they had seen no one leave but a very poorly dressed girl, who looked more like a peasant than a young lady.
When her two sisters came back from the ball, Cinderella asked them if they had enjoyed themselves again, and if the beautiful lady had been there:
they told her yes, but that she had run away when midnight struck, and so fast that she had dropped one of her little glass slippers, the prettiest in the world;

that the king's son had picked it up and had done nothing but look at it for the rest of the ball, and that he was certainly very much in love with the beautiful person the little slipper belonged to.
They spoke the truth; for a few days later the king's son had it announced to the sound of trumpets that he would marry the girl whose foot fitted the slipper exactly.
They began by trying it on the princesses, then on the duchesses and the whole court; but in vain.
It was brought to the two sisters, who did all they could to get their feet into the slipper; but they couldn't manage it.
Cinderella, who was watching them and recognised her slipper, said laughing: Let me see if it might fit me!
Her sisters burst out laughing and made fun of her.
The gentleman who was trying on the slipper, having looked closely at Cinderella and finding her very beautiful, said that this was only fair, and that he had orders to try it on every girl.
He sat Cinderella down and, bringing the slipper to her little foot, saw that it slipped on without any effort and fitted as if it had been made of wax.
The two sisters were greatly astonished, but even more so when Cinderella took the other little slipper out of her pocket and put it on her foot.
At that moment the godmother arrived and, tapping Cinderella's clothes with her wand, made them even more magnificent than all the others.
Then her two sisters recognised her as the beautiful person they had seen at the ball.
They threw themselves at her feet to beg her forgiveness for all the ill treatment they had made her suffer.
Cinderella raised them up and told them, as she embraced them, that she forgave them with all her heart and begged them to love her always.
She was taken to the young prince, dressed as she was.
He found her more beautiful than ever, and a few days later he married her.
Cinderella, who was as good as she was beautiful, gave her two sisters rooms at the palace, and that very same day married them to two great lords of the court.

That is what her godmother gave Cinderella,
By training her, by teaching her,
So well that she made her a queen;
For that is the moral we draw from this tale.
pt: Era uma vez um fidalgo que casou em segundas núpcias com uma mulher, a mais altiva e a mais orgulhosa que alguma vez se vira.
Ela tinha duas filhas do mesmo feitio, que se pareciam com ela em tudo.
O marido, por seu lado, tinha uma filha jovem, mas de uma bondade sem igual; herdara-a da mãe, que fora a melhor pessoa do mundo.
Mal se fez o casamento, a madrasta deixou rebentar o seu mau génio: não suportava as boas qualidades desta menina, que tornavam as suas filhas ainda mais odiosas.
Encarregou-a dos trabalhos mais baixos da casa: era ela que lavava a loiça e as escadas, que esfregava o quarto da senhora e os das meninas suas filhas;

dormia lá no alto da casa, num sótão, num miserável enxergão de palha, enquanto as irmãs tinham quartos com soalho de parquê, onde havia camas da última moda e espelhos em que se viam dos pés à cabeça.
A pobre rapariga aguentava tudo com paciência e não se atrevia a queixar-se ao pai, que ralharia com ela, porque a mulher o governava por completo.
Quando acabava o seu trabalho, ia sentar-se ao canto da lareira, no meio das cinzas, e por isso lhe chamavam vulgarmente Cu-de-Cinza.
A mais nova, que não era tão malcriada como a mais velha, chamava-lhe Gata Borralheira.
Mesmo assim, a Gata Borralheira, com as suas roupas velhas, era cem vezes mais bonita do que as irmãs, embora elas andassem vestidas com toda a magnificência.
Aconteceu que o filho do rei deu um baile e convidou todas as pessoas de qualidade.
As nossas duas meninas também foram convidadas, pois davam nas vistas na região.
Ei-las muito contentes e muito ocupadas a escolher os vestidos e os penteados que melhor lhes ficariam.
Mais trabalho para a Gata Borralheira; pois era ela que passava a roupa das irmãs e lhes engomava os punhos.
Só se falava da maneira como cada uma se havia de vestir.
— Eu — disse a mais velha — vou levar o meu vestido de veludo vermelho com o meu enfeite de renda inglesa.
— Eu — disse a mais nova — só vou levar a minha saia de todos os dias; mas, em compensação, ponho o meu manto com flores de ouro e o meu colar de diamantes, que não é nada de se deitar fora.
Mandaram chamar a melhor cabeleireira para lhes armar os toucados de duas fiadas e compraram sinais postiços à melhor fabricante.
Chamaram a Gata Borralheira para lhe pedir a opinião, pois ela tinha bom gosto.
A Gata Borralheira aconselhou-as o melhor que se podia e até se ofereceu para as pentear, o que elas aceitaram de bom grado.
Enquanto as penteava, elas diziam-lhe: Gata Borralheira, gostavas de ir ao baile?
— Ai, meninas, estão a troçar de mim; isso não é para mim.
— Tens razão; toda a gente se ria se visse uma Cu-de-Cinza ir ao baile.
Qualquer outra que não a Gata Borralheira tê-las-ia penteado mal de propósito; mas ela era bondosa e penteou-as na perfeição.
Passaram quase dois dias sem comer, tão grande era a alegria.
Rebentaram mais de doze cordões de tanto os apertarem para lhes afinar a cintura, e estavam sempre em frente ao espelho.
Por fim, chegou o feliz dia: partiram, e a Gata Borralheira seguiu-as com os olhos enquanto pôde.
Quando deixou de as ver, desatou a chorar.
A madrinha, que a viu lavada em lágrimas, perguntou-lhe o que tinha.
— Eu queria tanto…
Chorava tanto que não conseguiu acabar.
A madrinha, que era fada, disse-lhe: Querias tanto ir ao baile, não é verdade?
— Ai, queria — disse a Gata Borralheira, suspirando.
— Pois bem, vais portar-te bem? — disse a madrinha. — Eu faço-te ir.
Levou-a para o seu quarto e disse-lhe: Vai ao jardim e traz-me uma abóbora.
A Gata Borralheira foi logo apanhar a mais bonita que encontrou e levou-a à madrinha, sem conseguir adivinhar como é que aquela abóbora a poderia levar ao baile.
A madrinha escavou-a e, deixando só a casca, tocou-lhe com a varinha, e a abóbora transformou-se logo numa bela carruagem toda dourada;
depois foi ver a ratoeira, onde encontrou seis ratinhos todos vivos.

Disse à Gata Borralheira para levantar um pouco a porta da ratoeira e, a cada ratinho que saía, dava-lhe um toque com a varinha, e o ratinho transformava-se logo num belo cavalo, o que fez uma bela parelha de seis cavalos de um bonito cinzento-rato malhado.
Como estava sem saber de que havia de fazer um cocheiro, a Gata Borralheira disse: Vou ver se há alguma ratazana na armadilha; fazemos dela um cocheiro.
— Tens razão — disse a madrinha —, vai ver.
A Gata Borralheira trouxe-lhe a armadilha, onde havia três grandes ratazanas.
A fada escolheu uma das três, por causa dos seus magníficos bigodes; e, depois de lhe tocar, ela transformou-se num cocheiro gordo, com um dos mais belos bigodes que alguma vez se viram.
Depois disse-lhe: Vai ao jardim; encontrarás seis lagartos atrás do regador; traz-mos.
Mal ela os trouxe, a madrinha transformou-os em seis lacaios, que subiram logo para trás da carruagem com as suas fardas agaloadas e lá se seguravam como se nunca tivessem feito outra coisa na vida.
A fada disse então à Gata Borralheira: Pois bem! Aqui tens com que ir ao baile; não estás contente?
— Estou, mas vou assim, com estes trapos feios?
A madrinha só lhe tocou com a varinha e, no mesmo instante, a sua roupa transformou-se num vestido de tecido de ouro e prata, todo bordado de pedras preciosas;
depois deu-lhe um par de sapatinhos de cristal, os mais bonitos do mundo.

Quando ficou assim vestida, subiu para a carruagem, mas a madrinha recomendou-lhe acima de tudo que não passasse da meia-noite, avisando-a de que, se ficasse no baile um momento mais, a carruagem voltaria a ser abóbora, os cavalos ratinhos, os lacaios lagartos, e a sua roupa velha voltaria a ser o que era.
Ela prometeu à madrinha que não deixaria de sair do baile antes da meia-noite.
Lá vai ela, louca de alegria.
O filho do rei, a quem foram avisar que acabava de chegar uma grande princesa que ninguém conhecia, correu a recebê-la;
deu-lhe a mão à descida da carruagem e levou-a para a sala onde estavam todos.
Fez-se então um grande silêncio; deixou-se de dançar e os violinos pararam de tocar, tão atentos estavam todos a contemplar a grande beleza da desconhecida.
Só se ouvia um murmúrio confuso: Ah, como é bonita!
O próprio rei, apesar de velho, não deixava de olhar para ela e de dizer baixinho à rainha que havia muito tempo que não via uma pessoa tão bonita e tão encantadora.
Todas as senhoras estavam atentas ao seu penteado e à sua roupa, para terem iguais logo no dia seguinte, desde que se encontrassem tecidos suficientemente belos e artesãos suficientemente hábeis.
O filho do rei pô-la no lugar de honra e depois levou-a a dançar.
Dançou com tanta graça que a admiraram ainda mais.
Serviram uma ceia muito boa, da qual o jovem príncipe não comeu nada, tão ocupado estava a contemplá-la.
Ela foi sentar-se ao pé das irmãs e fez-lhes mil gentilezas:
repartiu com elas as laranjas e os limões que o príncipe lhe tinha dado, o que as espantou muito, porque não a reconheciam.
Enquanto a admiravam assim, a Gata Borralheira ouviu dar as onze e três quartos: fez logo uma grande vénia a todos e foi-se embora o mais depressa que pôde.
Assim que chegou, foi ter com a madrinha; e, depois de lhe agradecer, disse-lhe que gostava muito de ir outra vez ao baile no dia seguinte, porque o filho do rei lho tinha pedido.
Enquanto contava à madrinha tudo o que se tinha passado no baile, as duas irmãs bateram à porta: a Gata Borralheira foi abrir.
— Que demora a voltar! — disse-lhes ela, bocejando, esfregando os olhos e espreguiçando-se como se tivesse acabado de acordar.
No entanto, não tivera vontade nenhuma de dormir desde que se tinham separado.
— Se tivesses ido ao baile — disse-lhe uma das irmãs —, não te terias aborrecido:
apareceu a princesa mais bonita, a mais bonita que alguma vez se poderá ver;
foi muito amável connosco, deu-nos laranjas e limões.
A Gata Borralheira estava louca de alegria.
Perguntou-lhes o nome dessa princesa; mas elas responderam que ninguém a conhecia;
que o filho do rei estava muito aflito com isso e que daria tudo no mundo para saber quem ela era.
A Gata Borralheira sorriu e disse-lhes: Então era mesmo muito bonita!
Meu Deus, que sorte vocês têm!
Não a poderia eu ver?
Ai, menina Javotte, empreste-me o seu vestido amarelo, aquele que usa todos os dias.
— Ora essa! — disse a menina Javotte. — Era o que faltava!
Emprestar o meu vestido a uma Cu-de-Cinza imunda como tu! Tinha de estar mesmo doida.
A Gata Borralheira já esperava esta recusa e ficou contente com ela; pois teria ficado muito embaraçada se a irmã tivesse aceitado emprestar-lhe o vestido.
No dia seguinte, as duas irmãs foram ao baile, e a Gata Borralheira também, mas ainda mais bem vestida do que da primeira vez.
O filho do rei esteve sempre ao pé dela e não parou de lhe dizer palavras doces.
A jovem não se aborrecia nada e esqueceu-se do que a madrinha lhe tinha recomendado;
de tal maneira que ouviu a primeira badalada da meia-noite quando julgava que ainda nem eram onze horas;
levantou-se e fugiu tão ligeira como uma corça.
O príncipe seguiu-a, mas não a conseguiu apanhar.
Ela deixou cair um dos sapatinhos de cristal, que o príncipe apanhou com todo o cuidado.

A Gata Borralheira chegou a casa muito ofegante, sem carruagem, sem lacaios e com a sua roupa velha, sem lhe ter ficado nada de toda a sua magnificência a não ser um dos sapatinhos, o par daquele que tinha deixado cair.
Perguntaram aos guardas da porta do palácio se não tinham visto sair uma princesa:
disseram que não tinham visto sair ninguém a não ser uma rapariga muito mal vestida, que tinha mais ar de camponesa do que de menina.
Quando as duas irmãs voltaram do baile, a Gata Borralheira perguntou-lhes se se tinham divertido outra vez e se a bela senhora lá tinha estado:
disseram-lhe que sim, mas que tinha fugido quando deu a meia-noite, e tão depressa que deixara cair um dos seus sapatinhos de cristal, o mais bonito do mundo;
que o filho do rei o tinha apanhado e não fizera outra coisa senão olhar para ele o resto do baile, e que de certeza estava muito apaixonado pela bela pessoa a quem pertencia o sapatinho.
Disseram a verdade; pois, poucos dias depois, o filho do rei mandou anunciar ao som de trombetas que casaria com aquela cujo pé servisse bem no sapatinho.
Começaram a experimentá-lo nas princesas, depois nas duquesas e em toda a corte; mas em vão.
Levaram-no a casa das duas irmãs, que fizeram tudo o que podiam para meter o pé no sapatinho; mas não conseguiram.
A Gata Borralheira, que estava a olhar para elas e reconheceu o seu sapatinho, disse a rir: Deixem-me ver se não me serve a mim!
As irmãs desataram a rir e a troçar dela.

O fidalgo que fazia a prova do sapatinho, depois de olhar com atenção para a Gata Borralheira e de a achar muito bonita, disse que era justo e que tinha ordens para o experimentar em todas as raparigas.
Mandou sentar a Gata Borralheira e, aproximando o sapatinho do seu pezinho, viu que entrava sem esforço e lhe servia como se fosse de cera.
O espanto das duas irmãs foi grande, mas ainda maior quando a Gata Borralheira tirou do bolso o outro sapatinho e o calçou.
Nisto chegou a madrinha, que, dando um toque com a varinha na roupa da Gata Borralheira, a tornou ainda mais magnífica do que todas as outras.
Então as duas irmãs reconheceram nela a bela pessoa que tinham visto no baile.
Atiraram-se aos seus pés para lhe pedir perdão por todos os maus-tratos que a tinham feito sofrer.
A Gata Borralheira levantou-as e disse-lhes, abraçando-as, que lhes perdoava de bom coração e que lhes pedia que gostassem sempre dela.
Levaram-na ao jovem príncipe, vestida como estava.
Ele achou-a ainda mais bonita do que nunca e, poucos dias depois, casou com ela.
A Gata Borralheira, que era tão boa como bonita, deu às duas irmãs alojamento no palácio e, nesse mesmo dia, casou-as com dois grandes senhores da corte.

Foi isso que a madrinha deu à Gata Borralheira,
Educando-a, ensinando-a,
Tanto e tão bem que fez dela uma rainha;
Pois é esta a moral que deste conto se tira.
